papers.title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.first_page: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement E XPERIENCE -H ANDOFF R EINFORCEMENT L EARNING FOR R ECURSIVE S ELF -I MPROVEMENT Doyoung Kim1 , Byeongguk Jeon2 , Kailin Zhang1 , Sherry Yang1 1 New York University 2 KAIST AI {doyoungkim,sherryyang}@nyu.edu A BSTRACT arXiv:2611.16409v1 [cs.LG] 12 Nov 2026 It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Re- inforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment informa- tion to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task- local playbooks. Our method, ACE-RL, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook cu- rator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, ACE-RL achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit. papers.title: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost
papers.first_page: The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost Yitong Zhang1 Ang Li2 Yisen Wang2 1 School of Physics, Peking University 2 State Key Lab of General Artificial Intelligence, School of Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University arXiv:2611.13524v1 [cs.LG] 10 Nov 2026 Abstract Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the RSI Tax as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta- Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with mean total-token savings of 65.6–71.0%. We decompose the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods, verification accounts for 74.8–93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures: improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task stream. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents use tools to perform software development and other professional tasks [1–4]. Duri … carries into subsequent tasks. We focus on RSI with fixed model weights and distinguish methods by the components they update. One category of RSI maintains an evolving set of memories or skills for use in later tasks [8– 10]. Another category modifies the agent’s harness, including the instructions, tool interfaces, and control code used for task execution [11–13]. The self-improvement process has a cost of its own. Recent studies compare online auxiliary modules and task-level search under resource constraints, and relate capability gains to learning cost [14–16]. Validation-task selection and the amortization of skill-search cost are also studied [17, 18]. On a task stream, each update incurs a cost before its value for later tasks is known. Task execution itself also varies in token demand across tasks, runs, and models [19]. We call the token cost of the self-improvement process the RSI Tax. We count the tokens spent attempting an update even when the agent ultimately retains its previous state. End-to-end cost is the sum of these update tokens and the tokens used to execute the task stream. The two terms are coupled: an update can shorten later executions, but can also add context or induce longer trajectories. The relevant trade-off is between the agent’s capability gains over the task stream and this combined token cost. We compare six methods on repository and terminal task streams using two backbone models. Our simple baseline, Simple Reflection with Notes (SRN), revises one bounded note from completed failures without candidate search. Across the four model–environment settings, SRN matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI while using 65.6–71.0% fewer total tokens on average, depending on the comparison method (Figure 1). 1

papers.title: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses
papers.first_page: Asking the right question is key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses Hu Cang1,∗ 1 Department of Developmental and Cell Biology, University of California, Irvine, CA 92697, USA. ∗ e-mail: cangh@uci.edu Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) scientists pursue discovery through a chain of hypotheses, fitting candidate models to existing observations and often choosing experiments where those models disagree most. Yet when arXiv:2611.19841v1 [cs.AI] 15 Nov 2026 early data miss a narrow feature, model selection favors simple curves that agree across the unmeasured gap, so disagreement-guided search has no reason to look where the new phenomenon lies. When we tested two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, across 32 closed-loop trials with a narrow peak omitted from the starting data, both sampled inside the peak region less often than random search. Surprisingly, the agent that followed model disagreement more closely missed the peak in all 32 trials, whereas discovery succeeded when experiments probed the unmeasured gap early and followed up across the anomaly. Asking the right question, rather than testing only where current models disagree, is therefore key to AI discovery in a chain of hypotheses. Introduction Scientific inquiry advances through a chain of hypotheses: investigators propose explanations for what they have observed, run experiments to test them, and revise their models when measurements depart from expectation1–4 . Autonomous language-model agents can now run this loop end to end, proposing hypotheses and choosing which experiments to perform next5–9 . Most efforts to improve AI scientists have focused on building stronger equation and code generators10–13 on the assumption that the best next experiment is simply one that distinguishes among current candidate models. In classical experimental design and active learning, a standard strategy is measuring where the leading models disagree most14–20 . Yet measuring where models disagree works only when those models already differ where new phenomena lie21–23 . Early in an investigation, sparse observations can miss a localized feature altogether, and standard model selection penalizes extra parameters until the data show a clear departure24 . Simple models fitted to the observed background then agree across the unmeasured gap and differ only over minor details elsewhere. Following their disagreement steers experiments away from that gap rather than into it, much as confirmation bias keeps human researchers testing what their working theories already anticipate25–27 . To test how experimental choices shape autonomous discovery, we evaluated two frontier AI scientists, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1-Sol, in closed-loop equation-discovery trials where a narrow peak lay inside an initially unmeasured region. Both agents probed that region less often than random search, and the agent that followed equation disagreement more closely missed the peak in every trial as it spent its budget separating nearly identical background curves. By contrast, discovery succeeded when experiments entered the unmeasured gap early, detected a clear anomaly, and completed a multi-step chain of hypotheses across the peak. Asking the right question is therefore critical to AI discovery. 1

As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40× faster than the benchmark’s reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem’s PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4× as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6×. papers.title: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback
papers.first_page: SkillDuet: Co-Evolving Models and Skills through Response Feedback Xingguang Ji, Ziqiang Dong, Yubo Zhang, Xi Leng, Ninghua Yang, Yang Yang, and Guanjun Jiang Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba Abstract. During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model’s behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model’s sub- sequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model’s capabilities evolve, previously beneficial arXiv:2611.12109v2 [cs.AI] 12 Nov 2026 skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates pa- rameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model’s responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further pa- rameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, re- spectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their con- tent and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model–skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvem … ugh SFT or RL. Textual skills can play both roles at once, serving as supervision for parameter updates and as guidance for future tasks. Recent work extracts retrievable, editable skills from interaction trajectories or distills their guidance into model parameters during RL [1, 2, 3]. Other methods consolidate lessons across trajectories or refine skill documents using execution feedback [4, 5]. However, a skill that provides useful supervision for the current parameter update may not remain use- ful as guidance for the updated model’s subsequent interactions. A skill may become redundant once the model acquires the capabilities it supports. Other skills may remain useful, but their relevance can decline as the model’s behavior changes. Retained skills may also conflict with newly learned behavior or existing guidance. Retained skills therefore need to be reassessed throughout training in light of both their content and the model’s changing capabilities. Coordinating skill selection and refinement with parameter updates is central to skill-level recursive self-improvement (RSI), yet the two routes are usually studied separately. Coupling them is diﬀicult: the model changes at every step, judging a skill’s value through task execution is expensive, and the training objective itself provides no criterion for deciding which skills remain worth retaining. Two observations from our experiments motivate this need for reassessment. On ALFWorld, guidance extracted from earlier trajectories substantially improves task completion early in training. When the guid- ance remains fixed, its gains diminish as training progresses, with a negative mean gain in the final stage (Section 3.1). papers.title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
papers.first_page: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks Daoan Zhang1,∗ , Qinbo Bai1,∗ , Dehai Min2,∗ , Xingyu Mu3 , Ziyi Chen1 , Jianing Yin1 1 ByteDance Inc., USA 2 University of Illinois Chicago 3 New York University ∗ Equal Contribution Abstract arXiv:2611.13336v1 [cs.AI] 9 Nov 2026 The effectiveness of a self-improving system relies heavily on the quality of its verifier, which judges the outcome of each improvement round. However, the verifiers of most tasks are written by hand, which is expensive and does not scale to tasks that come without one. We propose Veritas, a harness that generates verifiers automatically. Unlike general-purpose agent harnesses, Veritas adds three mechanisms for verifier generation: an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles, partly refined by a self-improvement loop. We evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution, whose official verifiers we first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses. With the model fixed, the verifiers Veritas generates agree better with the official verdicts than those of seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks. On the two pairwise benchmarks they are at or near the best. They also agree better than those of the vendor’s own harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms also improve 9 of 12 harness–benchmark pairs scored by execution across three harnesses. Contact: Daoan Zhang (dwan.zhang@icloud.com) 1 Introduction Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which an AI system produces the next version of itself or of its own tooling, has moved from a thought experiment to working systems: agents that rewrite their own code or harness raise their SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench scores [33, 51, 68, 75], and scheduling heuristics found by AlphaEvolve now run in Google’s production infrastructure [18, 41]. Every one of these loops selects its next version by a verdict on each attempt, and in all of them the verifier is a program that existed before the loop started, such as a benchmark’s unit tests or a hand-written metric [41, 59]. This has two consequences. First, a task that comes without a verifier, as most tasks collected from real-world use do, cannot enter the loop until someone writes one, which is slow and expensive. Second, a task that does come with a verifier enters the loop with that verifier’s verdicts taken as they are, since the loop has no other way to tell whether an attempt succeeded. If the verifier has a flaw, the loop optimizes the flaw rather than the task, a failure known as reward hacking. Both training-time and test-time self-improvement have been described as “gated by the same bottleneck: the verifier” [67]. Benchmark verifiers do have such flaws, even after costly expert review. When 93 developers screened 1,699 SWE-bench tasks, 61.1% were flagged for tests that could reject valid solutions and 68.3% were discarded; the 500-task SWE-bench Verified was drawn from the rest [42]. A year later, 26 of those 500 still had tests that accepted wrong patches [70]. Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench Pro and τ -bench went through the same cycle of release, external audit and repair [11, 13, 37, 45, 53, 61, 69, 72], and an exploit that solved no task scored 100% on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench, because the official verifier ran its tests in a container that the agent or its patch could modify, and trusted their output [64]. 1

papers.first_page: AUTOA SSUMPTION : S EARCHING OVER A SSUMPTIONS D ISCOVERS ML-S YSTEMS A LGORITHMS Igor Sadalski 1 Minghao Guo 1 Benjamin Jones 1 Wojciech Matusik 1 A BSTRACT Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: specula- tive decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design arXiv:2611.14844v1 [cs.AI] 10 Nov 2026 choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share. We present AIOA, a framework that brings this approach to the numerical algorithms of atomistic simulation: an agent improves an algorithm against a pre-specified metric in a loop guarded by verifiers it cannot alter. Applied to ASE, a widely used atomistic simulation library, AIOA targets two facets of an algorithm: its implementation, rewritten to run faster with unchanged results, and the method itself, redesigned to converge with fewer force evaluations. Agents made six kernels 22–24 times faster on average in Python with NumPy and SciPy. On unseen problems, optimizers from the best configuration needed 3.1–3.4 times fewer force evaluations than L-BFGS for structure relaxation and 4.6–17 times fewer than standard climbing-image nudged elastic band calculations for reaction paths. The agents’ optimizers also contain two algorithmic components we did not find in the literature. Atomistic simulation rests on a small set of numerical algorithms shared by a vast number of calculations 1 . Their cost has two sources: the implementation, which sets how fast a given computation runs, and the method itself, which sets how much computation is needed, for example how many force evaluations a structure relaxation 2,3 , a reaction-path search 4 or a molecular- dynamics run 5 requires. Domain experts have refined both by hand for decades 6–8 , and any improvement propagates to every calculation downstream. Coding agents built on large language models could now take on part of this refinement. Placed in automated loops that propose code changes, measure them and keep the improvements, such agents have found more efficient matrix-multiplication schemes 9 and sped up numerical kernels 1.3- to 2.8-fold when coupled to a compiler or profiler 10–12 . Karpathy’s autoresearch 13 reduces such a loop to its essentials: an agent edits a training script and keeps the edit only if the validation loss falls. In autoresearch and other loops, pass rates on held-out tests can trail those on visible tests by tens of percentage points 22 . When evidence rejects h, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce C ONTRASTIVE Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, 89% of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve 73% of these candidates to a specific alternative. LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accu- mulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and ﬁtness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps arXiv:2611.15309v1 [cs.AI] 11 Nov 2026 what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers archi- tecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the bound- aries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm- design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark … volve, EvoX, and their successors (Cemri et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Du et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xing et al., 2026) keep asking how to build a better algorithm for assembling each iteration’s context. Propose stays a single LLM call inside that context and has little autonomy of its own. It sees only what the controller assembles, so harder problems, such as end-to-end optimization of an industrial code repository, stay out of reach. The judge boundary weakens as well. One agent’s lesson from a single attempt goes straight into the memory every other agent reads. No independent owner checks whether it holds, how far it should travel, or when it should expire, so the search narrows before the evidence justiﬁes it. The second cost is computational. By discovering this structure through interaction and environmental feedback, an agent can reuse what it learns on later tasks. papers.first_page: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions Pulkit Yadav Independent Researcher pulkityadav1@gmail.com arXiv:2611.17632v1 [cs.AI] 13 Nov 2026 Abstract Generating an evaluation suite from an agent’s specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements × personas × scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search’s product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a τ 2 -bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect’s traced footprint holds b scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most b/N to a suite of N . For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold θ = 0.10, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator’s own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property. 1 Introduction An agent’s specification (policy, tool schemas, routing rules, prompts) changes weekly while its evaluation suite is written once. A widely adopted response is to generate the suite from it: extract requirements, generate personas, cross them into scenarios, grade against predicates [8]. Read as search this is a familiar object: the generator fills a descriptor space, the suite is viewed as a descriptor-indexed archive [11, 13], and the argument for it is the argument for divergent search: coverage beats optimisation of a single objective [9]. The archive is then scored like a benchmark: run every scenario, average, compare. The mean over a diverse archive is dominated by the cells where nothing interesting happened. We ask what that mismatch costs when the question is practical (did this suite notice that the agent regressed?), answering it with mutation testing [4, 5] over controlled defects injected into a τ 2 -bench agent [16, 2]. The answer is not that the search is bad, but that coverage and score are misaligned in a way computable from baseline results alone, before the defect is introduced: for most defects the ceiling on the defect-attributable signal already sits below the detection threshold. Contributions. We formulate generated suites as diversity-driven search and give a coverage measure over the generator’s own descriptors, with a ceiling bounding what suite-level scoring can detect (§3.3); show over 7 defects and two domains that the ceiling binds for 4 of 5 traceable defects, and that a defect can saturate its ceiling while the suite-level pass rate moves the opposite way (§4.1); 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). papers.title: The Critic Can Hurt: On the Safety of Critics in LLM-Guided AutoML Search
papers.first_page: T HE C RITIC C AN H URT: O N THE S AFETY OF C RITICS IN LLM-G UIDED AUTO ML S EARCH Gaoyuan Du1 Xiaoyang Liu1 Rex Zhou1 Dengdu Jiang1 Rong Fu2 Meng Ding3 Defu Cao4 1 2 Amazon Independent Researcher arXiv:2611.19037v1 [cs.LG] 14 Nov 2026 3 4 University of Massachusetts Boston University of Southern California A BSTRACT LLM critics increasingly steer iterative search in agentic AutoML, prompt optimization, and self- refinement—evaluated for whether they help, but rarely for whether they can hurt. We isolate the critic’s marginal effect through a four-arm audit and characterize the loop’s tolerance through controlled fault injection. We show a naive 8B critic drives search below the no-critic random-search floor on 7 of 8 tabular datasets, losing up to 0.245 AUC in the worst case; the magnitude varies strongly with dataset, frontier, and budget. When: stronger critics attenuate the loss on the evaluated suite, without establishing a universal capability threshold. Why: controlled fault injection shows that non-directional errors are nearly costless under best-so-far search, whereas directional errors consume finite search opportunities; an idealized effective-sample calculation yields a necessary condition, q(m−1) > β, not a deployment certificate. How: a simple observable validation gate and a learned detector can reduce realized loss, but neither is guaranteed to preserve the full-budget no-critic baseline. We will release C RIT FAULT, to our knowledge the first benchmark for detecting harmful critic feedback in AutoML. A critic is not a free addition: audit before trusting, and gate when capability or verification is insufficient. Keywords LLM critics · critic safety · iterative LLM-guided search · automated machine learning · LLM-as-a-judge 1 Introduction Automated machine learning (AutoML) searches over preprocessing, feature transformations, model families, and hyperparameters to build predictive pipelines with minimal human effort [10, 12, 42, 52]. Recent agentic systems [4, 17, 26, 54] organize this search as a propose–evaluate–correct loop: a proposer selects a candidate pipeline, the candidate is scored on held-out data, and an LLM critic converts the score and search history into recommendations that condition the next proposal, while the system retains a best-so-far incumbent. In principle, critique buys sample efficiency [19]. We show that it can do the opposite: a naive LLM critic can drive search below the floor of using no critic at all. We study the critic rather than the proposer because the two fail asymmetrically. A weak proposal is evaluated, scores poorly, and is discarded by the best-so-far rule; the loop verifies proposals by construction. A critique receives no such check: it is typically neither scored nor filtered, yet it conditions every subsequent proposal. Its cost is therefore not a degraded incumbent—elitist selection protects what has already been found—but sustained misdirection of a finite evaluation budget away from configurations that unguided search would otherwise reach. Evidence from adjacent settings suggests this risk is real but leaves it unmeasured. LLMs often fail to self-correct without an external signal [22], reported gains concentrate where a verifier is available [27], and LLM-as-judge scores are biased and unstable [51, 63]; verbal self-refinement reports similarly uneven results [37, 48]. That evidence, however, concerns one-shot judgment, whose cost is bounded by a single decision. Closed-loop evaluations, in turn, ablate feedback to measure how much it helps (e.g., SELA’s search-policy ablation [4]); existing evaluations rarely test the implicit harmlessness assumption directly against an otherwise identical loop with the critic removed.

papers.first_page: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents Subodh Lonkar Independent Researcher Abstract arXiv:2611.16378v1 [cs.AI] 12 Nov 2026 Autonomous agents increasingly modify prompts, memories, tool configurations, workflows, and control policies in response to interaction histories. The ability to generate a plausible modification, however, does not establish that it should become persistent system state. Candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect or manipulable, and repeated local improvements can conceal degradation relative to an earlier operating baseline. This paper develops Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a statistical and operational framework for governing persistent adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audit samples, requires practically meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies mandatory governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. The statistical contribution is an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent, candidate-specific calibration samples that compare the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference evaluation procedure. A reproducible Monte Carlo stress test illustrates the importance of calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is explicitly a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The paper does not claim empirical validation on a real autonomous-agent system. papers.title: Ballad: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery
papers.first_page: BALLAD: Bandit-Based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery Samidha Verma1 Ankit Anand2 Sayan Ranu1 1 2 Indian Institute of Technology Delhi McGill University arXiv:2611.17241v2 [cs.AI] 13 Nov 2026 Abstract Modern automated heuristic discovery (AHD) systems increasingly rival hand- crafted heuristics by leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively mutate and refine solutions. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics. We challenge this empir- ically: across multiple NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models. This raises a deeper ques- tion: given a pool of LLMs spanning frontier and freely hosted or open-weight models, how should one adaptively select which model to invoke at each step of the search? The challenge is non-trivial. The optimal LLM may shift over the course of a run, and because one LLM’s output seeds the context for subsequent calls, each model’s reward signal is non-stationary and entangled across the heuris- tic population, thus violating the independence assumptions of classical online decision-making settings. We address this through BALLAD (Bandit-based LLM Routing for Automated Heuristic Discovery), an online bandit algorithm that learns to orchestrate a pool of LLMs into an ensemble that matches or exceeds what any soloist LLM achieves alone. This orchestration is powered by an LLM selection policy that favors rare, high-scoring heuristics over stable averages, a DAG-based credit propagation mechanism through the genealogy of the heuristic population, and discounting of stale observations to remain attuned to each model’s current utility. Across five NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems and a pool of four models of varying capability and cost, BALLAD not only matches the best in- dividual LLM, but in several cases surpasses every individual model, while reducing API cost by up to 65.6% relative to always using the strongest model. 1 Introduction and Related Works Heuristics for hard combinatorial problems have traditionally been designed by human experts, a process that is slow, domain-specific, and difficult to scale. Recent works have shown that Large Language Models (LLMs) based systems such as FunSearch [18], EoH [15], and AlphaEvolve [16] iteratively prompt an LLM to mutate and refine heuristics expressed as code, achieving performance that rivals or exceeds hand-crafted solutions on a range of combinatorial problems. A practical bottleneck is cost. Automated heuristic discovery (AHD) requires thousands of LLM calls per run, making the choice of model a first-order concern. A natural assumption is that more powerful and more expensive models consistently yield better heuristics, justifying the overhead. We challenge this assumption directly: across five combinatorial optimization benchmarks, we find no consistent advantage for larger, costlier models, and in several cases smaller or free models outperform their expensive counterparts. This finding has an immediate practical implication: rather than committing to a fixed model or a fixed ensemble that pays for every model on every round, one should adaptively select which LLM to invoke at each step, based on online feedback from the search itself. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).

Most existing methods, however, rely on fixed schedules or scalar measures of progress, leaving nonstationary skill demands unaddressed. We propose SPG-Select, a framework for allocating limited practice budget using a multidimensional profile inferred from binary outcomes via MIRT. The framework predicts surrogate progress, defined as the difference between consecutive profile estimates, and prioritizes progress in dimensions with larger estimated proficiency gaps. Our SPG-Select-R policy combines these predictions with uncertainty-based exploration and periodic restarting to accommodate nonstationarity. We evaluate SPG-Select on ALFWorld and WebShop with three skill-evolution backends. In the reported runs, SPG-Select-R achieves higher mean held-out terminal success than uniform sampling in all six backend-benchmark combinations, with gains of 1.49-13.18 percentage points on ALFWorld and 0.93-3.13 points on WebShop. Under a predictable linear surrogate model and boundedness assumptions, we establish a high-probability dynamic pseudo-regret bound for surrogate task allocation in terms of parameter path variation. 1.
